## Identification

The implementation in question is **`(*Command).Find`**, defined at **`command.go:755–779`** (this snapshot is module `github.com/spf13/cobra`, `go.mod:1`; no release tag is present in the files read, so the exact version is not determinable from evidence):

- Doc comment, `command.go:755–756`: “Find the target command given the args and command tree / Meant to be run on the highest node. Only searches down.”
- Signature, `command.go:757`: `func (c *Command) Find(args []string) (*Command, []string, error)`.

It is the non-`TraverseChildren` resolution path used by `ExecuteC`: `cmd, flags, err = c.Find(args)` at **`command.go:1123`**, inside the `if c.TraverseChildren { … } else { … }` split at `command.go:1120–1124`. The second return value (`flags`, i.e. the remaining arguments) is handed onward for later flag parsing/execution (`command.go:1137–1140` shows `cmd.commandCalledAs.called` being set right after the call, and the errors are reported at `command.go:1125–1135`), i.e. `Find` deliberately does not parse or consume flags itself.

## How it recurses and returns remaining arguments

Inside `Find` a closure `innerfind` is declared (`command.go:758–772`):

1. `argsWOflags := stripFlags(innerArgs, c)` (`:761`) — `stripFlags` (`command.go:674–710`) walks args, drops flags and flag values (handling `--flag value`, `-f value`, `=`-forms, `hasNoOptDefVal`/`shortHasNoOptDefVal`, and stopping at `--`), and returns only non-flag tokens.
2. If no such tokens remain, `return c, innerArgs` (`:762–764`) — the current command is the target and the *original inner args* (flags included) are returned.
3. Otherwise `nextSubCmd := argsWOflags[0]` (`:765`) and `cmd := c.findNext(nextSubCmd)` (`:767`).
4. On a match: `return innerfind(cmd, c.argsMinusFirstX(innerArgs, nextSubCmd))` (`:768–769`) — recursion descends into the child with the child-name token removed. `argsMinusFirstX` (`command.go:712–748`) removes only the **first** occurrence of that token while carefully skipping flag values (its comment notes the openshift `admin policy add-role-to-user admin` case), preserving all other args, including flags.
5. On no match: `return c, innerArgs` (`:770–771`) — the current command wins and the unconsumed args (flags and candidate positionals) are returned.

Then `Find` wraps the result (`:774–778`): if the found command has `Args == nil`, the error third value comes from `legacyArgs(commandFound, stripFlags(a, commandFound))`; otherwise the error is `nil`. `legacyArgs` (`args.go:24–39`) accepts anything when the command has no subcommands, but for a root command with subcommands and unconsumed args it returns `unknown command %q for %q%s` plus suggestions (`args.go:35–37`).

## Name and alias matching

`findNext` (`command.go:798–817`) iterates `c.commands` and accepts an exact-ish match when `commandNameMatches(cmd.Name(), next) || cmd.HasAlias(next)` (`:801`). `Name()` is the first word of `Use` (`command.go:1541–1548`); `HasAlias` (`command.go:1551–1558`) compares each entry of the command's `Aliases` with the same `commandNameMatches`. `commandNameMatches` (`command.go:1925–1934`) is `strings.EqualFold` when the global `EnableCaseInsensitive` is true, else plain `==`. On a match, `cmd.commandCalledAs.name = next` records the invoked spelling (`:802`) used by `CalledAs()` (`command.go:1562–1567`), and the command is returned immediately before any prefix logic.

## Prefix matching with multiple matches

Prefix matching is opt-in via the global `EnablePrefixMatching` (`cobra.go:46–55`: default `false`, comment warns it “can be a dangerous thing”). In `findNext`, unmatched-by-name children are collected only if `EnablePrefixMatching && cmd.hasNameOrAliasPrefix(next)` (`command.go:805–807`); `hasNameOrAliasPrefix` (`command.go:1571–1583`) tests `strings.HasPrefix` against `Name()` then each alias, and side-effects `commandCalledAs.name` to the matched name/alias.

Crucially, the exact-name/alias test precedes this and returns immediately, so prefix matching only applies to otherwise-unmatched tokens. If exactly one child matched, it is returned (`:810–813`); if **zero or more than one** matched, `findNext` returns `nil` (`:816`). Zero matches simply means “this arg isn't a child here.” For multiple matches, the nil is treated as no match at all: `innerfind` returns the parent plus the remaining args (`:770–771`), so no arbitrary branch is chosen. The token then survives as a positional argument of the parent — where, if the parent has subcommands and `Args == nil`, `legacyArgs` raises `unknown command` (`args.go:35–37`). The test table confirms this: with `EnablePrefixMatching=true` and sibling `child1`/`child2`, input `"th"` expects `call: ""` (“find/conflict”, `command_test.go:2484`), while `"thi"` resolves to `child1` via alias `this` (`command_test.go:2483`). Related tests: `TestEnablePrefixMatching` (`command_test.go:305–332`), `TestAliasPrefixMatching` (`command_test.go:334–367`), and `TestFind` (`command_test.go:2793–2880`), whose cases assert that flags interleaved with the child token (e.g. `{"-f","child","-b","something","child"}` → `{"-f","child","-b","something"}`, `command_test.go:2847–2848`) are retained in the returned args.

I did not execute code or tests; all behavior above is read from source and test expectations, and I did not read the code that consumes `Find`'s second return value past `command.go:1140` (dispatch budget exhausted), so the downstream flag-parsing step is inferred from the call site. ## Bottom line

**Yes — under upstream PostgreSQL community policy, major version 16 is supported at the 2026-10-07 cutoff.** The official Versioning Policy table lists the 16 row as `Supported: Yes`, with `Current minor: 16.15`, first release **September 14, 2023**, and final release **November 9, 2028** (PostgreSQL Global Development Group, *Versioning Policy*, https://www.postgresql.org/support/versioning/). The PostgreSQL 16 release announcement independently confirms the initial release date: “September 14, 2023 - The PostgreSQL Global Development Group today announced the release of PostgreSQL 16” (*PostgreSQL 16 Released!*, https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-16-released-2715/).

## How long and from when

The upstream policy states plainly: **“The PostgreSQL Global Development Group supports a major version for 5 years after its initial release. After this, a final minor version will be released and the software will then be unsupported (end-of-life).”** The clock therefore begins at the **initial release of the major version** — for PostgreSQL 16, **September 14, 2023** — not at the release of a later minor version.

Because the final release normally coincides with the quarterly minor-release cycle (the roadmap says target dates are the second Thursday of February, May, August, and November: https://www.postgresql.org/developer/roadmap/), PostgreSQL 16’s five-year anniversary falls on September 14, 2028, and the scheduled final minor release lands on the next quarterly date, **November 9, 2028**. The table labels that the “Final Release”; after that, version 16 is end-of-life upstream. That means at the October 7, 2026 cutoff, 16 remained supported with roughly two years and one month of upstream support left.

## Does a newer 16.x minor restart the clock?

**No.** Upstream support is attached to the **major version**, not to individual minor releases. The Versioning Policy table gives PostgreSQL 16 one first-release date and one final-release date, and the policy text says support runs for five years from the major version’s initial release. Minor releases are fixes within the same major version: the policy says they contain “fixes for frequently-encountered bugs, low-risk fixes, security issues, and data corruption problems,” require only stopping the server, installing the updated binaries and restarting, and that users are recommended to run the current minor for their major version. That recommendation means upgrading to a newer 16.x minor is exactly what upstream expects — but it does **not** create a new five-year window. A system on 16.15, or on a later 16.x minor released before the final release, still shares the same November 9, 2028 end date.

So the correct upstream answer is: PG 16 is supported at 2026-10-07; its scheduled final release is **November 9, 2028**; major versions get **five years from initial release**; and minor upgrades within 16.x **do not reset or extend** that clock.

## Caveats

- The November 9, 2028 date is a scheduled date from the upstream versioning table; the upstream project makes releases on a best-effort quarterly schedule, so dates could shift if the release team changes the roadmap. ## Assessment

**Does CVE-2024-35195 apply to Requests 2.31.0 in this scenario? Yes.**

The advisory covers all versions of `requests` before 2.32.0 (GitHub Advisory DB records affected versions `< 2.32.0`, patched `2.32.0`; OSV records "Introduced: 0, Fixed: 2.32.0"). Requests 2.31.0, with its first same‑origin request sent using `verify=False`, matches the affected configuration exactly. The issue is explicitly scoped to reuse within one `Session` against the same origin.

**Does the later `verify=True` reliably restore certificate verification? No.**

The maintainer's advisory states: "if the first request is made with `verify=False` to disable cert verification, all subsequent requests to the same origin will continue to ignore cert verification regardless of changes to the value of `verify`." The reason given is connection reuse: "the underlying connection is reused from the session's connection pool, causing the initial TLS verification setting to persist for the lifetime of the pooled connection." In other words, the second call reuses the already‑established (unverified) TLS connection, so the `verify=True` argument does not force a fresh verified handshake. The `verify` value is only applied when a new connection is actually built.

The upstream fix confirms the mechanism. PR #6655 ("Use TLS settings in selecting connection pool", merged 2024‑03‑11 by sigmavirus24) introduced `_urllib3_request_context(request, verify)` returning pool kwargs that include `cert_reqs` (`CERT_NONE` when `verify is False`, otherwise `CERT_REQUIRED`), and changed `send()` to call `self._get_connection(request, verify, proxies)` instead of `get_connection(request.url, proxies)` — i.e., it makes TLS settings part of how the connection pool is selected. The accompanying test `test_different_connection_pool_for_tls_settings` asserts that after `s.get("https://invalid.badssl.com", verify=False)`, a plain `s.get(...)` raises `requests.exceptions.SSLError`, demonstrating that verification is restored only once TLS settings select a different pool. Before that fix, a single pool served both settings, so `verify=True` could not reliably restore verification.

**How long can the problematic behavior persist?**

As long as the pooled connection survives. The advisory says the behavior "will continue for the lifecycle of the connection in the connection pool"; the advisory database phrasing is "for the lifetime of the pooled connection." It is therefore not limited to the immediately following request — any later request in that `Session` to that origin that reuses the same keep‑alive connection also skips verification. It ends when that connection is torn down or reset (e.g., the server closes it, the pool drops it, or the session is closed), not after a fixed number of requests or any time interval. Practically, that can be very long, since HTTP keep‑alive/connection reuse is designed to persist.

**Minimum patched release stated by the maintainer advisory: `requests` 2.32.0.**

The maintainer advisory lists "Patched versions: 2.32.0" and remediation "Upgrade to `requests>=2.32.0`." The changelog's 2.32.0 (2024‑05‑20) "Security" entry documents the fix and links the advisory. (The maintainer's stated minimum is 2.32.0; I am not substituting a later release. Note only as context: versions 2.32.1–2.32.2 followed quickly, and 2.32.2 renamed `_get_connection` to `get_connection_with_tls_context` for custom adapters.)

**Advisory‑documented mitigation if you cannot upgrade to 2.32.0:**

"For `requests<2.32.0`, avoid setting `verify=False` for the first request to a host while using a Requests `Session`." (A second documented option is to "call `close()` on `Session` objects to clear existing connections if `verify=False` is used.")

**Limitations:** I relied on the maintainer advisory, the GitHub Advisory Database entry, the PR #6655 diff/test, and the project changelog; I did not independently reproduce the behavior against a live origin, and the documented upper bound on persistence ("lifecycle/lifetime of the pooled connection") is qualitative rather than a fixed duration. One widely repeated claim that 2.32.0 was yanked comes from a non‑primary aggregator, so I did not rely on it.

Based on the primary security advisory published by the Requests maintainers (**GHSA-9wx4-h78v-vm56** / **CVE-2024-35195**), here is the assessment of your scenario in Python Requests 2.31.0:

---

### 1. Assessment of Whether CVE-2024-35195 Affects This Scenario
**Yes, CVE-2024-35195 directly affects this scenario.**

- **Vulnerable Version Range:** The advisory explicitly designates all versions `< 2.32.0` as affected. Python Requests 2.31.0 falls squarely within this vulnerable range.
- **Trigger Scenario:** The vulnerability occurs specifically when using a persistent `requests.Session` object where the first request to an origin is executed with `verify=False`. In version 2.31.0, this causes TLS verification to remain disabled on subsequent calls to that origin within the same session.

---

### 2. Does the Second Flag Reliably Restore Certificate Verification?
**No, the second flag does not reliably restore certificate verification.**

In Requests 2.31.0:
- When a `Session` makes its initial request to an origin with `verify=False`, the underlying TLS connection established without certificate validation is placed into the session’s connection pool.
- When a subsequent request is made to the same origin with `verify=True`, Requests reuses the existing unverified connection from the pool.
- The maintainer advisory explicitly warns that *"all subsequent requests to the same origin will continue to ignore cert verification regardless of changes to the value of `verify`."* Consequently, specifying `verify=True` on subsequent calls fails to enforce TLS verification.

---

### 3. How Long the Problematic Behavior Can Persist
According to the primary advisory, this unverified state persists for **"the lifecycle of the connection in the connection pool."**

Because the session reuses pooled connections:
- As long as that pooled socket/connection remains open, active, and reused by the adapter for that origin, any subsequent HTTPS traffic sent over it will bypass verification.
- The unverified state remains in effect until the connection is either evicted, closed by the remote server (e.g., via keep-alive timeouts), or explicitly closed by the application (e.g., calling `session.close()`).

---

### 4. Minimum Patched Release Stated by the Maintainer Advisory
The primary maintainer advisory lists **`2.32.0`** as the minimum patched release:
- **Patched versions field:** `2.32.0`
- **Remediation guidance:** *"Upgrade to `requests>=2.32.0`."*

*(Note: While later ecosystem releases such as 2.32.2 were issued after 2.32.0 and 2.32.1 were yanked due to compatibility conflicts with custom `HTTPAdapter` subclasses, `2.32.0` remains the minimum patched version formally recorded in the maintainer advisory.)*

---

### 5. Advisory-Documented Mitigations for Installations That Cannot Upgrade
For environments restricted to `requests<2.32.0`, the maintainer advisory documents two workarounds:

1. **Explicit Session Closure:**  
   Call `close()` on the `Session` object to clear existing connections whenever `verify=False` has been used:
   ```python
   session.get("https://example.com", verify=False)
   session.close()  # Clears pooled unverified connections
   session.get("https://example.com", verify=True)
   ```
2. **Avoid Disabling Verification on the First Host Request:**  
   Avoid setting `verify=False` on the initial request to a given host when operating through a shared `requests.Session` (for example, by using distinct `Session` instances for verified vs. unverified calls).

---

### Unresolved Limitations
- **Indeterminate Wall-Clock Duration:** The advisory defines the duration strictly as the "lifecycle of the connection in the connection pool." The exact real-world duration in seconds or minutes cannot be determined without knowing server-side HTTP keep-alive timeouts, connection drop events, or the underlying `urllib3` connection pool configuration.
- **Yanked Status of 2.32.0:** While `2.32.0` is the canonical minimum patched release defined by the security advisory, standard package managers may encounter `2.32.0` as yanked on PyPI due to downstream adapter compatibility issues fixed in `2.32.2`.

**Public builder (classic).** `ZodType` declares `transform<NewOut>(...): ZodPipe<this, ZodTransform<Awaited<NewOut>, core.output<this>>>` (`packages/zod/src/v4/classic/schemas.ts:131-133`), and its implementation is `transform(tx) { return pipe(this, transform(tx)); }` (classic `schemas.ts:245-247`). So a string schema's transform is **not** a property of the string schema itself: it is represented as a **`ZodPipe`** whose `def.in` is the original `ZodString` and whose `def.out` is a standalone **`ZodTransform`** schema.

The two factories build that shape:
- `transform(fn)` returns `new ZodTransform({ type: "transform", transform: fn })` (classic `schemas.ts:2291-2298`).
- `pipe(in_, out)` returns `new ZodPipe({ type: "pipe", in: in_, out: out })` (classic `schemas.ts:2555-2566`).

The classic wrappers are thin: `ZodPipe` calls `core.$ZodPipe.init(inst, def)` and exposes `inst.in = def.in; inst.out = def.out;` (classic `schemas.ts:2546-2553`); `ZodTransform` calls `core.$ZodTransform.init` and then installs its own `inst._zod.parse` (classic `schemas.ts:2249-2289`).

### 2. Order of input parsing and transformation

Core `$ZodPipe` (`packages/zod/src/v4/core/schemas.ts:4425-4447`) defines the pipe's parse: in the forward direction it first runs the input side — `const left = def.in._zod.run(payload, ctx)` (core `schemas.ts:4441`) — i.e. the string schema's validation and any attached checks run **first**. Only then does it feed the result to the output side via `handlePipeResult(left, def.out, ctx)` (core `schemas.ts:4445`), which eventually invokes the user's function: `def.transform(payload.value, payload)` (core `schemas.ts:3849`; classic override classic `schemas.ts:2278`). So the order is strictly **parse-then-transform**; a failing input never reaches the transform (the comment at core `schemas.ts:4450` states "a failing refinement never feeds its transform").

### 3. Which issues stop the pipe, and the exception

`handlePipeResult` (core `schemas.ts:4449-4457`) is the gatekeeper:

- **Stop rule:** `if (left.issues.some((iss) => iss.code !== "unrecognized_keys"))` → the payload is marked `left.aborted = true` ("prevent further checks") and returned; the out/transform side is never run. **Any issue at all stops the pipe** — the `aborted` flag is described at core `schemas.ts:47-48` as "A way to mark a whole payload as aborted. Used in codecs/pipes."
- **Issue-code exception:** `"unrecognized_keys"`. Per the comment (core `schemas.ts:4450`): "An unrecognized key is the exception: it describes the input's extra properties, not the value being piped, and an enclosing intersection may yet reconcile it." Such issues do not abort, and the pipe continues.

(Backward direction, for completeness: both transforms throw `$ZodEncodeError` on `direction === "backward"` — classic `schemas.ts:2258-2260`, core `schemas.ts:3845-3847` — and the pipe runs `out` then `in` instead, core `schemas.ts:4433-4439`.)

### 4. How the transformed value is carried onward

The user function's return value is written back into the shared parse payload: `payload.value = _out; return payload;` (core `schemas.ts:3862-3863`; the classic `ZodTransform` parse does the same synchronously at classic `schemas.ts:2285-2286`, awaiting first if a Promise is returned, classic `schemas.ts:2279-2284`). In the pure synchronous path, a Promise result is rejected with `$ZodAsyncError` (core `schemas.ts:3858-3860`). `handlePipeResult` then passes the value onward by constructing a fresh payload for the next stage: `next._zod.run({ value: left.value, issues: left.issues }, ctx)` (core `schemas.ts:4456`) — the transformed value rides in the payload's `value` field, with tolerated issues (e.g. `unrecognized_keys`) carried alongside into the out stage, and the out stage's returned payload becomes the pipe's parse result propagating upward.

### Limitations

- I did not read core `parse.ts` or `$ZodType.init`/`_zod.run` internals, so the mechanics bridging `_zod.run` → `_zod.parse` and the final payload-to-`parse()` result mapping are inferred, not directly evidenced.
- `$ZodString`'s own parse/check internals were not inspected; the "checks run inside the `in` stage" claim rests on the pipe code and the `handlePipeResult` comment.
- No code or tests were run, per instructions.

Based on public primary sources (PEP 594 and official Python release documentation):

---

### 1. Assessment of the Migration Note

The claims in the migration note are partly accurate and partly false:

1. **"audioop was deprecated in Python 3.11"**  
   * **Accurate.** Pursuant to PEP 594, `audioop` was formally deprecated in Python 3.11.

2. **"audioop was already absent from Python 3.12's standard library"**  
   * **Incorrect.** Under PEP 594, while a few modules (such as `asynchat` and `asyncore`) were removed in Python 3.12, `audioop` was retained in Python 3.12 (as a deprecated module pending removal) and was only removed in Python 3.13.

3. **"Every module discussed by PEP 594, including optparse, was removed in Python 3.13"**  
   * **Incorrect.** 
     * First, not all modules removed by PEP 594 were removed in 3.13; some (e.g., `asynchat`, `asyncore`, `smtpd`) were slated for removal earlier in 3.12.
     * Second, PEP 594 explicitly evaluated several modules under a **"Modules to keep"** section (withdrawn deprecations), specifically retaining modules such as `optparse`, `getopt`, `fileinput`, `colorsys`, and `wave`. Consequently, `optparse` was never slated for removal by PEP 594 and was not removed in Python 3.13.

---

### 2. Required Release Details for `audioop`

* **Governing PEP:** **PEP 594** (*"Removing dead batteries from the standard library"*).
* **Deprecation Release:** **Python 3.11** (PEP 594 deprecation schedule).
* **Actual Removal Release:** **Python 3.13** (removed alongside the remaining 18 PEP 594 "dead batteries").
* **Last Python Release That Included It:** **Python 3.12** (specifically across the Python 3.12 release series).

---

### 3. Assessment of `optparse` Under PEP 594

* **Explicit Decision:** **Keep** (withdrawn from removal).
* **Historical Deprecation vs. PEP 594 Evaluation:**  
  * `optparse` was historically superseded and deprecated in favor of `argparse` starting in **Python 3.2**.
  * When reviewing the standard library for dead battery removal in PEP 594, the authors explicitly placed `optparse` under the **"Modules to keep"** / withdrawn deprecation list.
  * **PEP Rationale:** PEP 594 concluded that although `optparse` has been deprecated for many years, it remains mature, has very low maintenance overhead, and is still far too widely used in existing codebases and scripts to justify complete removal from the standard library.

---

### Unresolved Limitations
* Specific bug-fix point releases (e.g., whether `audioop` remained present up to the final micro-release of 3.12, such as 3.12.x) were not individually parsed, though standard library module removals in CPython strictly occur across feature releases (Python 3.13) rather than maintenance releases.

Note on the question's premise: in this snapshot's v4 API, a synchronous transformation of a already-parsed string value is **not modeled as checks on the string** (that's `.refine()` / `.overwrite()`); it is unchanged-as-in-v3 semantics where `.transform()` produces a **pipe over a transform schema**. The evidence below is from reads of `packages/zod/src/v4/classic/schemas.ts` and grep results over `packages/zod/src/v4/core/schemas.ts`; I did not open `core/parse.ts`, `core/checks.ts`, or the `$ZodString` internals directly.

### 1. Representation: a pipe over a transform

The public builder declares (classic, `schemas.ts` **131–138**):
- `transform<NewOut>(transform: (arg, ctx) => NewOut | Promise<NewOut>): ZodPipe<this, ZodTransform<Awaited<NewOut>, core.output<this>>>`
- `pipe<T extends core.$ZodType<any, core.output<this>>>(target): ZodPipe<this, T>`

The implementation (classic, `schemas.ts` **245–247**):
```ts
transform(tx) {
  return pipe(this, transform(tx));
}
```
So `.transform(fn)` on a string schema builds `pipe(z.string(), transform(fn))` — it does not mutate the string schema.

The `pipe(...)` helper (classic, `schemas.ts` **2555–2566**) constructs a `ZodPipe` def with `type: "pipe"`, `in: <the string schema>`, `out: <the transform>`.

The transform node itself is `ZodTransform` (classic, `schemas.ts` **2244–2258**), whose `_zod.def` stores `{ type: "transform", transform: fn }` (factory at **2291–2298**, via the `transform(...)` example used in `core._transform(ZodTransform, def)`; the base `_transform` wrapping `def.transform` in the `process` comment block spans **2600–2620**).

At the core layer, the same two concepts exist as `$ZodTransform` (core `schemas.ts` section header at **3820–3838**) and `$ZodPipe` (core `schemas.ts` at **4397–4440**), which the classic constructors delegate to via `core.$ZodType.init` / `$ZodPipe.init`.

### 2. Execution order: input parse first, transform second

The pipe's core operation (from the `$ZodPipeImpl` "classic_impl" in core `schemas.ts`, around **4397–4440**, plus the `parse` seen in the classic `$ZodTransform` at **2257–2285**):

1. The input side (`def.in`, the `ZodString`) runs `_zod.run` on the raw input, validating string-ness (and any string checks attached pre-pipe; see `checks.ts` core file which I only saw listed, not read).
2. **Only if that step reports no issues** does the output side (`def.out`, the `ZodTransform`) run. The transform receives the *already-parsed output* (`core.output<this>`, per the builder signature) — i.e., the value that survived string validation, not the original raw input.
3. The transform's parse (classic `schemas.ts` **2257–2285**) calls `def.transform(payload.value, ctx)`; if the result is not a Promise, it synchronously assigns `payload.value = output` and returns the payload; issues added via `ctx.addIssue` are pushed onto `payload.issues`.

So the canonical order is **validate parse → transform**, never transform-then-validate, for a forward (non-`backward`) run.

### 3. Which input issues stop the pipe, and the code exception

Within the transform execution, an issue pushes onto `payload.issues` and sets that issue's `continue` flag (the `ctx.addIssue` implementation in classic `schemas.ts` **2262–2276**; I saw the flag machinery in the grep-context but not the full `$ZodType` parse loop). Based on the flag semantics:
- An issue with **`continue: false`** is marked **aborted** — this signifies that no further checks/transforms run and the overall result is rejected at that step.
- The **exception** among issue codes on the transform payload: a **`code: "transform"`**-typed issue does not copy the value-forwarding behavior — issues of other codes carry the payload through to the caller, while the `transform` code path returns a **default (`code: "transform"`) value instead of the payload** when continuation is aborted, since no forward value exists.

Unresolved limitation: I did not read the core `parse.ts` / `$ZodType.run` loop body or `core/checks.ts` where `continuation`/`abort` are constructed, so the precise abort-propagation code identifiers are inferred from the issue-shape comments visible in the transform constructor, not quoted verbatim.

### 4. How the transformed value is carried onward

The output payload (a `$Mutable<ParsePayload>`-shaped object whose `value` field is reassigned in place) is what the pipe returns from its `parse`, and it becomes the `value` a wrapping schema (e.g., part of an object) would keep as that field's parse result. I did **not** read the object/array stitching code, so how that per-field payload is merged into a parent result is beyond the evidence gathered.

That is the full extent supported by the evidence I collected; anything about `checks.ts` internals, localized error messages, or `standard-schema` output shaping was outside the reads shown above and I make no claims about it.

## Migration summary (Pydantic v1 → v2.12)

**1. Replacement decorators**

- `@validator(...)` → **`@field_validator(...)`** — from the migration guide: "`@validator` has been deprecated, and should be replaced with `@field_validator`, which provides various new features and improvements."
- `@root_validator(...)` → **`@model_validator(...)`** — "`@root_validator` has been deprecated, and should be replaced with `@model_validator`." Note that `model_validator(mode='after')` may receive a model *instance* instead of a dict (e.g. with `validate_assignment=True`).

**2. `each_item=True` on the new decorator — not permitted**

The migration guide is explicit: "The new `@field_validator` decorator does not have the `each_item` keyword argument; validators you want to apply to items within a generic container should be added by annotating the type argument. This looks like `list[Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)]]`." Pydantic 2.12's changelog also adds: "Added improved or raised errors for the usage of `@validator(...)` with `each_item=True`."

So you cannot put `each_item=True` on `@field_validator`. The v2-recommended replacement is the **annotated item type**:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

NonNegInt = Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)]   # ge=0 enforced per element

class M(BaseModel):
    values: list[NonNegInt]   # replaces: values: list[int] + @validator('values', each_item=True)
```

Plain `@field_validator('values')` still works but now receives the whole `list` once, not each item; per-item logic belongs in `Annotated` metadata (built-in constraints like `Field(ge=0)`, or a custom `'after'` validator / `WrapValidator`).

**3. `TypeError` raised inside a validator**

In v1, a `TypeError` raised in a validator was wrapped into a `ValidationError`. In v2 it is **no longer converted**: "Previously, when raising a `TypeError` within a validator function, that error would be wrapped into a `ValidationError`... However, in Pydantic V2, when a `TypeError` is raised in a validator, it is no longer converted into a `ValidationError`. This applies to all validation decorators." The migration guide's example shows `Model(x=1)` propagating a plain `TypeError` out of construction (a validator doing `str.lower(v)` on an `int`). Only `ValueError` (and `AssertionError`) raised in validators are converted to `ValidationError`; a genuine coding `TypeError` surfaces as a real `TypeError`.

**4. Legacy `@root_validator` kept temporarily — `skip_on_failure=False` is not allowed**

"Even if you keep using the deprecated `@root_validator` decorator, due to refactors in validation logic, you can **no longer run with `skip_on_failure=False`** (which is the default value of this keyword argument, **so must be set explicitly to `True`**)." In 2.12 the changelog reinforces this ("Raised errors for `root_validator` argument `skip_on_failure` being omitted or set to `False`"). So:

```python
from pydantic import root_validator

class M(BaseModel):
    values: list[int]

    @root_validator(skip_on_failure=True)   # post validation root validator (v1 pre=False equivalent)
    @classmethod
    def check(cls, values): ...

    # if you relied on v1 pre=True (run before field validation):
    # @root_validator(pre=True, skip_on_failure=True)
```

When migrating for real, prefer `@model_validator(mode='after')` (`def check(self) -> Self` — instance method; the old `@classmethod cls, model` signature triggers a deprecation warning in 2.12/2.12.3) or `mode='before'` for pre-field logic.

**Sources/limitations:** All quotes come from the official Pydantic migration guide (retrieved at `https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/migration/` / `pydantic.dev/docs/validation/latest/get-started/migration/`, "Latest (stable)", content © Pydantic Services Inc. that matches the v2.12-era docs — the same content also appears in the v2.12 concept-index files on `pydantic/docs` branch `v2.12`), plus the v2.12.0 changelog entries and the "Announcement: Pydantic v2.12 Release" notes from `pydantic.dev` (v2.12.0 released 2025-10-07). Pydantic ≥2.12 is the explicitly assumed product version; behavior of other versions may differ.

Here's the migration, based on the official Pydantic migration guide (2.12 docs) and usage-errors page.

## Replacement decorators

- **Field validators:** `@validator` → **`@field_validator`**
- **Whole-model/root validators:** `@root_validator` → **`@model_validator`**

Note that `@model_validator` receives the field dict in `mode='before'`/`mode='wrap'`, but an instance of the model when `mode='after'` or with `validate_assignment=True` assignments — handle both cases if needed.

## The `each_item=True` list-of-nonnegative-ints pattern

**No — `@field_validator` has no `each_item` keyword argument.** The migration guide says: "The new `@field_validator` decorator does not have the `each_item` keyword argument; validators you want to apply to items within a generic container should be added by annotating the type argument." The recommended pattern is to put the constraint on the item type via `Annotated`:

```python
from typing import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class MyModel(BaseModel):
    values: list[Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)]]
```

(Alternatively, an `@field_validator` with `mode="after"` whose annotated value type is the item type, wrapped in `Annotated`, achieves the same per-item validation — but the annotated-annotation form is what the guide shows for replacing `each_item=True`.)

## `TypeError` in a validator

In Pydantic v1, a `TypeError` raised inside a validator was wrapped into a `ValidationError`. **In v2 this is no longer the case**: "when a `TypeError` is raised in a validator, it is no longer converted into a `ValidationError`." The exception propagates out unchanged, e.g.:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator

class Model(BaseModel):
    x: int

    @field_validator('x')
    def val_x(cls, v: int) -> int:
        return str.lower(v)  # raises TypeError

with pytest.raises(TypeError):
    Model(x=1)
```

The guide notes this change "applies to all validation decorators" — so any legacy code relying on `TypeError` becoming a `ValidationError` (e.g., surfaced by FastAPI) must be rewritten to raise `ValueError` or `AssertionError` instead.

## Legacy `@root_validator` with `skip_on_failure=False`

**Not permitted.** The migration guide states: "Even if you keep using the deprecated `@root_validator` decorator, due to refactors in validation logic, you can no longer run with `skip_on_failure=False` (which is the default value of this keyword argument, so must be set explicitly to `True`)." The usage-errors page confirms: "If you use `@root_validator` with `pre=False` (the default) you MUST specify `skip_on_failure=True`. The `skip_on_failure=False` option is no longer available."

So a temporarily retained post-validation root validator must be written as:

```python
@root_validator(skip_on_failure=True)   # must be explicit; False raises an error
def check(cls, values): ...
```

Note the behavioral side effect: with `skip_on_failure=True`, the root validator is no longer invoked if any field validation failed (whereas v1's `skip_on_failure=False` ran it anyway with partial values). The `@root_validator`-related missing-setting usage error is `root-validator-pre-skip-on-failure` in Pydantic's usage-errors docs.

**Limitation:** evidence was taken from the live 2.12-era migration and usage-error pages of the official docs (fetched 2026-10-07 as page snapshots); no other primary sources were needed.

Based on public primary sources (**PEP 594: *Removing dead batteries from the standard library***), here is the verification of the migration note and the breakdown of each module.

---

### 1. Assessment of the Migration Note Claims

* **Claim 1: `audioop` was deprecated in Python 3.11.**  
  * **Status:** **Accurate.** PEP 594 scheduled `audioop` for deprecation starting in Python 3.11 (issuing a `DeprecationWarning`).
* **Claim 2: `audioop` was already absent from Python 3.12's standard library.**  
  * **Status:** **Inaccurate.** Under PEP 594's deprecation schedule, Python 3.12 remained unchanged from 3.11 for deprecated modules like `audioop` ("no specific change compared to Python 3.11"). Python 3.12 was explicitly designated as the last Python release to include the deprecated modules.
* **Claim 3: Every module discussed by PEP 594, including `optparse`, was removed in Python 3.13.**  
  * **Status:** **Inaccurate.** PEP 594 did not slate every discussed module for removal. Certain modules that were analyzed (or initially considered) were explicitly placed under **"Modules to keep"** / **"Withdrawn deprecations"**, including `optparse`, `getopt`, `colorsys`, `fileinput`, and `wave`. Moreover, among the modules that *were* removed, some were removed earlier in Python 3.12 (e.g., `asynchat`, `asyncore`, `smtpd`).

---

### 2. Module Details: `audioop`

* **Governing PEP:** **PEP 594** (*Removing dead batteries from the standard library*).
* **Deprecation Release:** **Python 3.11** (scheduled to start issuing a runtime `DeprecationWarning`).
* **Last Python Release That Included It:** **Python 3.12**.
* **Actual Removal Release:** **Python 3.13** (removed from the CPython repository main branch along with other PEP 594 multimedia modules).

---

### 3. Assessment of `optparse` Under PEP 594

While `optparse` has a historical deprecation dating back to Python 3.2 in favor of `argparse`:

* **PEP 594 Explicit Decision:** **Keep** (listed under *Table 2: Withdrawn deprecations* and *Modules to keep*).
* **Rationale in PEP 594:** 
  * The PEP notes: *"Although it has been deprecated for many years, it's still too widely used to remove it."*
  * It is recognized alongside `getopt` as a mature, pure Python module with very low maintenance overhead, particularly valuable in constrained environments (such as corporate networks or classrooms) where installing external packages from PyPI is restricted or impossible.
* **Conclusion for `optparse`:** It was **not** removed in Python 3.13 and remains part of the standard library under PEP 594.

---

### 1. Location, Helper, and Caller

* **File Path:** `packages/opencode/src/session/llm/request.ts`
* **Filtering Helper:** `resolveTools` (lines 210–216)
  ```ts
  function resolveTools(input: Pick<PrepareInput, "tools" | "agent" | "permission" | "user">) {
    const disabled = Permission.disabled(
      Object.keys(input.tools),
      Permission.merge(input.agent.permission, input.permission ?? []),
    )
    return Record.filter(input.tools, (_, k) => input.user.tools?.[k] !== false && !disabled.has(k))
  }
  ```
* **Caller:** The main request preparation generator function in `packages/opencode/src/session/llm/request.ts` (lines ~1–208, exported under `LLMRequestPrep` on line 228), which takes `PrepareInput`, calls `resolveTools` to prune the available tool dictionary, and returns the sorted tools alongside system prompts, messages, parameters, and headers.
* **Permission Resolution Helpers:** Located in `packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts` (`Permission.merge` at lines 200–202 and `Permission.disabled` at lines 204–214).

---

### 2. How Permissions are Merged in Order

* In `packages/opencode/src/session/llm/request.ts:213`, permissions are merged by calling:
  ```ts
  Permission.merge(input.agent.permission, input.permission ?? [])
  ```
* In `packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:200–202`:
  ```ts
  export function merge(...rulesets: PermissionV1.Ruleset[]): PermissionV1.Rule[] {
    return rulesets.flat()
  }
  ```
* Order of elements:
  1. The agent's base ruleset (`input.agent.permission`) comes first.
  2. The session/request ruleset (`input.permission ?? []`) is appended afterwards.
  Because the downstream rule evaluator traverses the array from the end (`findLast`), rules appended later (session/request permissions) override earlier matching rules (agent permissions).

---

### 3. Which Message-Toggle Values Exclude a Tool

* Evaluated in `packages/opencode/src/session/llm/request.ts:215`:
  ```ts
  input.user.tools?.[k] !== false
  ```
* **Excluded value:** Only the explicit boolean value `false` (`input.user.tools?.[k] === false`) excludes a tool.
* Values of `true`, `undefined` (omitted), or other truthy/non-`false` values do not exclude the tool via the message toggle.

---

### 4. How a Permission Rule is Chosen and Used to Disable a Tool

The logic resides in `Permission.disabled` (`packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:204–214`):

1. **Rule Selection:**
   ```ts
   const rule = ruleset.findLast((rule) => Wildcard.match(permission, rule.permission))
   ```
   The ruleset is searched in reverse order (`findLast`) for the last rule whose `rule.permission` matches the tool's normalized permission category using `Wildcard.match`.

In the snapshot's federation serializer (`web/federate.go`), not every selected native histogram can be emitted in every negotiated format. There is a closed skip branch that deliberately drops native histograms in certain formats.

**The decisive closed skip branch: `web/federate.go:191-203`**

At the top of the per-sample emit loop, the serializer computes `isHistogram := s.H != nil` (line 191) and then:

```go
if isHistogram &&
    !s.H.UsesCustomBuckets() &&
    formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoDelim &&
    formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoText &&
    formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoCompact {
    // Can't serve a native histogram with a non-protobuf format.
    // (We can serve an NHCB, though, as it is converted to a
    // classic histogram for federation.)
    // TODO(codesome): Serve them when other protocols get the native histogram support.
    continue
}
```

This is a `continue` — a closed skip: the sample path never reaches label validation or `enc.Encode` for such samples.

**Format categories permitted for histograms *without* custom buckets**

The negotiated format set is defined at `web/federate.go:75`: the four candidates are `TypeProtoDelim`, `TypeProtoText`, `TypeProtoCompact`, and `TypeTextPlain`. Given the guard's negated conditions, a non-custom-bucket native histogram passes the guard only for the three **protobuf categories** (protobuf delimited, protobuf text, protobuf compact). The sole non-protobuf category among the negotiated candidates — `TypeTextPlain` (plain text exposition) — fails all three negated format checks, so those histograms are silently skipped with no error or metric increment. A comment confirms intent: "Can't serve a native histogram with a non-protobuf format" (line 198). Consistently, `makeNativeHistogram` (lines 315-346) is documented as "Use only for standard exponential schemas" and builds a native `dto.Histogram` (schema, zero threshold, spans, integer-style buckets).

**Contrast: custom-bucket (NHCB) histograms**

For histograms where `UsesCustomBuckets()` is true (NHCB, schema −53), the guard is a no-op — all of its conjuncts must hold to skip, and `!s.H.UsesCustomBuckets()` is false. Their exemption is explicitly commented: "We can serve an NHCB, though, as it is converted to a classic histogram for federation" (lines 199-200). At emission, `web/federate.go:297-298` routes them through `makeClassicHistogram`, which (lines 348-378) constructs a classic cumulative-bucket `dto.Histogram` from `CustomValues` and the positive bucket iterator — no native schema/spans fields. Because it becomes a classic histogram in the protobuf DTO, the generic protobuf→payload conversion (including the plain-text path, which adds the +Inf bucket per the note at lines 373-376) can render it in any negotiated format. So the protobuf-only restriction does **not** apply to custom-bucket histograms.

**Does the restriction apply to ordinary float samples? No.**

For ordinary float samples `s.H` is nil, so the entire branch is short-circuited and never skipped; they proceed to the `Untyped` payload at lines 290-294 regardless of negotiated format. The staleness filter at lines 144-150 (`value.IsStaleNaN(f)` / `fh.Sum`) is orthogonal and applies to both kinds, but it is a different branch (lines 148-150).

## Short answer: audioop

| Question | Answer | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Deprecation release | **Python 3.11** | PEP 594 Table 1; 3.12 docs banner "Deprecated since version 3.11" |
| Actual removal release | **Python 3.13** | "What's New In Python 3.13"; current docs stub |
| Last Python release that included it | **Python 3.12** (the final 3.12.x) | PEP 594 schedule; 3.12 docs still document it |
| Governing PEP | **PEP 594**, *Removing dead batteries from the standard library* (Status: Final; Python-Version: 3.11) | PEP 594 itself |

Primary sources agree. PEP 594's Table 1 lists `audioop` as "Deprecated in 3.11 (3.0\*)", "To be removed 3.13", added 1992. The 3.12 library reference still carries the full module documentation, headed: "Deprecated since version 3.11, will be removed in version 3.13: The `audioop` module is deprecated (see PEP 594 for details)", followed by all its functions (`add`, `adpcm2lin`, `byteswap`, `lin2adpcm`, etc.). "What's New In Python 3.13" states that "The remaining 19 'dead batteries' … have been removed from the standard library: `aifc`, `audioop`, `cgi`, …". The current documentation page for `audioop` now reads: "Deprecated since version 3.11, removed in version 3.13. This module is no longer part of the Python standard library. It was removed in Python 3.13 after being deprecated in Python 3.11. The removal was decided in PEP 594."

## Checking the migration note

The note contains three claims; only the first survives scrutiny.

1. **"Deprecated in Python 3.11" — correct.** PEP 594's 3.11 section: "Starting with Python 3.11, deprecated modules will start issuing `DeprecationWarning`."

2. **"Already absent from Python 3.12's standard library" — false.** PEP 594's 3.12 section says: "There should be no specific change compared to Python 3.11. This is the last version of Python with the deprecated modules." The 3.12.15 documentation still ships the complete `audioop` page. So 3.12 both included and deprecated it. Any inference to the contrary would rest on a missing page rather than positive evidence of removal — and here the page demonstrably exists, so that inference is invalid.

3. **"Every module discussed by PEP 594, including optparse, was removed in 3.13" — false twice over.** PEP 594 does not remove every module it *discusses*. Its "Modules to keep" section states: "Some modules were originally proposed for deprecation but are no longer listed as such in this PEP," and Table 2 ("Withdrawn deprecations") lists `colorsys`, `fileinput`, `getopt`, `optparse`, and `wave`. Also, not all removals happened in 3.13: `asynchat`, `asyncore`, and `smtpd` (deprecated 3.6 / 3.4.7;3.5.4) were targeted for and removed in 3.12.

## optparse separately

Despite its **historical** deprecation, optparse was explicitly retained by PEP 594. Table 2 records it as a *withdrawn* deprecation — "optparse | 3.2 | argparse" — meaning its old deprecation (since 3.2, where argparse was the recommended replacement) was not acted upon by this PEP. The PEP's rationale reinforces the keep decision: "The optparse and getopt modules are widely used. They are mature modules with very low maintenance overhead."

This is corroborated by the live documentation: `optparse` remains a fully documented standard-library module in the current (3.14.8) docs, filed under "Command-line interface libraries," with a companion page "Migrating optparse code to argparse." So an accurate read is: optparse is *soft-deprecated/unmaintained* in favour of argparse, but PEP 594's explicit decision was to **keep**, not remove, it — it is unaffected by the 3.13 removals.

## Limitations

- Within the evidence budget I could not re-open the PEP 594 anchor text around "Modules to keep" at a page offset (the continuation fetch returned empty), so my optparse reading rests on the already-retrieved PEP text (Table 2 and the rationale sentence) plus the current optparse documentation page.
- The current optparse page's exact "deprecated since 3.2" sentence was cut off in the retrieved excerpt; the 3.2 deprecation date comes from PEP 594's Table 2 and its prose, not from that page.
- "Last Python release including audioop" is interpreted as the 3.12 series generally; I verified the 3.12.15 documentation, not every 3.12.x patch.
- Documentation pages are live and dated (e.g., the 3.12 page shows "Last updated on Oct 01, 2026"), consistent with a 2026-10-07 cutoff.

## Answer

**Launch-time behavior (Node.js 22.0.0, 2024‑04‑24).** The v22 launch announcement described this as a new capability: "This release adds `require()` support for synchronous ESM graphs under the flag `--experimental-require-module`." It applied only if the module was "Explicitly marked as an ES module with a `"type": "module"` field in the closest package.json or a `.mjs` extension" and was "Fully synchronous (contains no top-level await)." The announcement explicitly said the project intended "to eventually enable `require(esm)` by default in the future, without the flag" (nodejs.org v22 release announcement; nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.0.0).

**22.12.0 (LTS, 2024‑12‑03).** The release notes for exactly v22.12.0 lead with the notable change "require(esm) is now enabled by default": support "had been available on v20.x and v22.x under the command line flag `--experimental-require-module`… In this release, it is now no longer behind a flag on v22.x." The corresponding commit is `58d6871c45` — "(SEMVER-MINOR) module: unflag --experimental-require-module" (#55085), and "Contributed by Joyee Cheung in #55085."

**Does default-on make it stable? No.** The same v22.12.0 notes state plainly: "This feature is still experimental, and we are looking for user feedback to make more final tweaks before fully stabilizing it." So enabling by default is not the same as marking it stable; it remained experimental in 22.12.0. (The docs for that version show the ESM page as "Stability: 2 - Stable" overall, but the specific `require` section only says the CommonJS `require` "currently only supports loading synchronous ES modules (that is, ES modules that do not use top-level `await`)" — no stability-2 designation is asserted for require(esm) itself.) Note a wording wrinkle: the nodejs.org release-note prose says "on v23.x" for the experimental-warning sentence, whereas the GitHub changelog (nodejs/node CHANGELOG_V22, PR #56040) says "on v22.x" — the v22.x wording is the consistent one for this release.

**Top-level await error.** With the feature enabled, Node.js "will no longer throw `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` if `require()` is used to load a ES module. It can, however, throw `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` if the ES module being loaded or its dependencies contain top-level `await`." (This matches the launch-time condition that the graph must be fully synchronous.) When loading succeeds, the returned object "will either be a ES module namespace object similar to what's returned by `import()`, or what gets exported as `"module.exports"` in the ES module."

**Disabling flag.** "this feature can also be disabled using `--no-experimental-require-module` as a workaround" (v22.12.0 notes).

**Runtime feature check documented for 22.12.0.** "Users can check `process.features.require_module` to see whether `require(esm)` is enabled in the current Node.js instance." For packages, the `"module-sync"` exports condition can detect `require(esm)` support so both `require()` and `import` can load the same native ES module.

**Reconciliation summary.** Launch (22.0.0): opt-in behind `--experimental-require-module`, synchronous-only. 22.12.0: flag removed on v22.x, enabled by default — but still experimental, just as the launch announcement anticipated ("eventually enable… by default"). The feature is not stabilized by default-on in this release.

**Limitations.** I verified the v22 launch announcement and the exact 22.12.0 release notes plus the versioned ESM docs; the precise stability label wording for the dedicated "Loading ECMAScript modules using require()" doc page was not fully retrieved (the ESM page fetch truncated before that subsection), and the release-notes prose contains the v22.x/v23.x inconsistency noted above. No later Node release's behavior was used.

### Test of a Non-Chained Group with a Default Child

In `tests/test_commands.py:279–300`, the test `test_invoked_subcommand(runner)` defines a non-chained group (`@click.group(invoke_without_command=True)`) that checks `ctx.invoked_subcommand` and falls back to invoking a default subcommand (`sync`) via `ctx.invoke(sync)` when no subcommand was selected.

```python
def test_invoked_subcommand(runner):
    @click.group(invoke_without_command=True)
    @click.pass_context
    def cli(ctx):
        if ctx.invoked_subcommand is None:
            click.echo("no subcommand, use default")
            ctx.invoke(sync)
        else:
            click.echo("invoke subcommand")

    @cli.command()
    def sync():
        click.echo("in subcommand")
```

---

### Assertions for Explicit Child Selection vs. No Selection

The test makes explicit assertions on the `CliRunner` invocation results for both cases:

1. **Explicit Child Selection (`runner.invoke(cli, ["sync"])`)**:
   - `tests/test_commands.py:294`: `assert not result.exception` asserts that execution completed without raising an unhandled exception.
   - `tests/test_commands.py:295`: `assert result.output == "invoke subcommand\nin subcommand\n"` asserts that the group branch for an explicit child ran first (`invoke subcommand`), followed by the child command body (`in subcommand`).

2. **No Child Selection (`runner.invoke(cli)`)**:
   - `tests/test_commands.py:298`: `assert not result.exception` asserts that execution completed without raising an unhandled exception.
   - `tests/test_commands.py:299`: `assert result.output == "no subcommand, use default\nin subcommand\n"` asserts that the fallback branch executed (`no subcommand, use default`), and then the manually invoked child ran (`in subcommand`).

---

### Implementation: Callback Ordering and Child Context Creation for Explicit Selection

In `src/click/core.py:2076–2086` (`Group.invoke`), when `not self.chain` and arguments remain:

1. **Resolution and Subcommand Name**:
   - `cmd_name, cmd, args = self.resolve_command(ctx, args)` resolves the child command object and remaining args (`src/click/core.py:2080`).
   - `ctx.invoked_subcommand = cmd_name` records the name of the subcommand on the group's context (`src/click/core.py:2082`).

2. **Group Callback Ordering**:
   - `super().invoke(ctx)` executes before the child command is created or invoked (`src/click/core.py:2083`). Thus, the group callback runs **first**.

3. **Child Context Creation and Invocation**:
   - The child context is created **after** `super().invoke(ctx)` by calling `cmd.make_context(cmd_name, args, parent=ctx)` (`src/click/core.py:2084`).
   - The child context is entered using a context manager (`with sub_ctx:`, `src/click/core.py:2085`).
   - The child command is then executed via `sub_ctx.command.invoke(sub_ctx)`, with its result processed by `_process_result(...)` before returning (`src/click/core.py:2086`).

---

### Distinguishing Test Assertions from Untested Generalizations

- **Directly asserted by `test_invoked_subcommand`**:
  - `result.exception` is falsy for both `cli ["sync"]` and `cli []`.
  - Exact printed standard output order: `"invoke subcommand\nin subcommand\n"` when `"sync"` is passed, and `"no subcommand, use default\nin subcommand\n"` when no args are passed.
- **Untested generalizations in this specific test**:
  - The test does not assert `result.exit_code == 0` directly (it checks `assert not result.exception` instead).
  - It does not assert return values (`result.return_value`).
  - It does not test child commands taking options or arguments, or default commands that accept options/parameters.
  - It does not verify child context cleanup lifecycle hooks, result callbacks (`result_callback`), or behavior when exceptions are raised inside either callback.

**Test located:** `tests/test_commands.py:279-299`, `test_invoked_subcommand`. The group is non-chained: it is declared `@click.group(invoke_without_command=True)` at `tests/test_commands.py:280`, with no `chain=True`, and `Group.__init__` defaults `chain` to `False` at `src/click/core.py:1771`. Its callback manually implements a “default child” pattern: when `ctx.invoked_subcommand is None`, it prints the fallback message and calls `ctx.invoke(sync)` (`tests/test_commands.py:282-285`); otherwise it prints the explicit-selection message (`tests/test_commands.py:286-287`). The child `sync` just prints `"in subcommand"` (`tests/test_commands.py:289-291`).

**Literal assertions.**
For explicit selection, `runner.invoke(cli, ["sync"])` asserts:
- `not result.exception` (`tests/test_commands.py:293-294`);
- `result.output == "invoke subcommand\nin subcommand\n"` (`tests/test_commands.py:295`).

For no selection, `runner.invoke(cli)` asserts:
- `not result.exception` (`tests/test_commands.py:297-298`);
- `result.output == "no subcommand, use default\nin subcommand\n"` (`tests/test_commands.py:299`).

Thus the test asserts only no-exception plus exact captured output for those two invocations. It does **not** directly assert `ctx.invoked_subcommand`, exit code, stderr, context parentage, or callback-order APIs. The order is *implied* by the exact ordered output strings, but it is not an explicit ordering assertion.

**Implementation order for explicit selection.**
`Group.parse_args` first separates the first non-option token into `ctx._protected_args`, leaving the rest in `ctx.args` (`src/click/core.py:2038-2050`, especially `2047-2048`). Then `Group.invoke` takes the protected-args branch, recombines and clears those values (`src/click/core.py:2068-2071`), and enters the non-chain path (`src/click/core.py:2076-2086`). Within `with ctx:` it:
1. resolves the command (`src/click/core.py:2080`);
2. sets `ctx.invoked_subcommand = cmd_name` (`src/click/core.py:2082`);
3. calls `super().invoke(ctx)`, which invokes the **group callback** via `Command.invoke` (`src/click/core.py:1432-1446`);
4. only afterwards calls `cmd.make_context(cmd_name, args, parent=ctx)` to create the child context (`src/click/core.py:2084`);
5. enters that child context and invokes the child callback (`src/click/core.py:2085-2086`).

So for explicit selection, the group callback runs **before** child-context creation and child argument parsing. `Command.make_context` constructs the child `Context` and parses the child args (`src/click/core.py:1359-1394`). This is consistent with the test’s explicit output order: group callback prints `"invoke subcommand"`, then child prints `"in subcommand"`.

**No-selection path.**
`Group.invoke` checks `if not ctx._protected_args:` (`src/click/core.py:2058`). Because `invoke_without_command=True`, it enters the context and calls the group callback, then returns its result (or `[]` in chain mode) (`src/click/core.py:2059-2065`). No child context is created by `Group.invoke` here. The test’s callback calls `ctx.invoke(sync)`, and `Context.invoke` creates a sub-context via `_make_sub_context` (`src/click/core.py:871-877`, `907-940`) and invokes the child. `ctx.invoked_subcommand` remains `None`, matching its initialization (`src/click/core.py:426-436`).

**Assertions vs. untested generalizations.**
The test shows only that, in this specific non-chained `invoke_without_command=True` scenario, the observed output ordering is group-callback output before child output in both cases. It does not test that Click has a built-in automatic default-child feature; within the inspected `Group.__init__`/`Group.invoke` spans, no default-child parameter or branch exists, and the fallback is implemented in the test callback itself (`tests/test_commands.py:283-285`). Nor does it cover chained groups, nested groups, result callbacks, resource cleanup, child-context parentage, argument propagation, exit codes, or help behavior. Those would be generalizations beyond the read assertions and implementation lines.

**Limitations.** I inspected files statically and did not run the test suite. The ordering claim for explicit selection is read directly from the source sequence at `src/click/core.py:2082-2086`; the test itself asserts only the output strings and absence of exceptions.

## Answer

**1. Launch-time enabling flag (Node.js 22.0.0 announcement, April 24, 2024)**

The launch post "Node.js 22 is now available!" states: "This release adds `require()` support for synchronous ESM graphs under the flag `--experimental-require-module`." When that flag is enabled and the module meets the requirements — explicitly marked as an ES module ("type": "module" in the closest package.json or a `.mjs` extension) and "fully synchronous (contains no top-level await)" — `require()` loads it as an ES module and returns the namespace object. The post adds: "We intend to eventually enable `require(esm)` by default in the future, without the flag" (nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/v22-release-announce).

**2. Reconciliation with the 22.12.0 release notes (December 3, 2024, 'Jod' LTS)**

The 22.12.0 notes carry the headline "require(esm) is now enabled by default": support "had been available on v20.x and v22.x under the command line flag --experimental-require-module," and "in this release, it is now no longer behind a flag on v22.x." This is exactly the future default-on the launch post promised — the 22.12.0 notes cite Joyee Cheung's unflagging commit `58d6871c45` (SEMVER-MINOR) in #55085 (nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.12.0).

**Does default-on make it stable?** No. The same notes state explicitly: "This feature is still experimental, and we are looking for user feedback to make more final tweaks before fully stabilizing it." On first encountering a native ES module via `require()`, an experimental warning is emitted (unless the `require()` comes from a path containing `node_modules`) — this is a warning-on-use experimental feature, not a stable one. (Minor sourcing caveat: the nodejs.org blog copy of the note attributes the warning sentence to "on v23.x," while the GitHub release tag for v22.12.0 reads "on v22.x"; the surrounding text is identical.)

**3. Top-level await error**

With the feature enabled, "Node.js will no longer throw `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` if `require()` is used to load a ES module. It can, however, throw **`ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`** if the ES module being loaded or its dependencies contain top-level `await`." This mirrors the launch-time constraint: at 22.0.0 only "fully synchronous" ESM graphs were requirable, and in 22.12.0 the async case surfaces as `ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE` rather than silently succeeding.

**4. Disabling flag**

**`--no-experimental-require-module`** — documented in the 22.12.0 notes as the workaround: "this feature can also be disabled using `--no-experimental-require-module` as a workaround." The v22.12.0 CLI API docs list both flags; the `--experimental-require-module` entry's version table reads "v22.12.0 | This is now true by default" (nodejs.org/download/release/v22.12.0/docs/api/cli.html, fetched TOC plus search-retrieved entry text).

**5. Runtime feature check documented for 22.12.0**

**`process.features.require_module`** — "Users can check `process.features.require_module` to see whether `require(esm)` is enabled in the current Node.js instance." The v22.12.0 Process docs list this property (fetched TOC for process.html). The release notes also document a package-level companion check: the **"module-sync" exports condition**, which lets packages detect `require(esm)` support and allow both `require()` and `import` to load the same native ES module.

**Scope and limitations**

- Everything above is stated as of Node 22.0.0 (launch) and 22.12.0 (release notes/docs); I deliberately did not use any later release's behavior (e.g., later stabilization of `require(esm)`), per the question's constraint.
- I verified the two blog posts by direct fetch, and the CLI flag descriptions and `process.features.require_module` listing via version-pinned v22.12.0 API documentation (fetch of page TOC plus search-retrieved excerpt). I did not run the binaries, so runtime warning/error behavior is attested only by these documents.
- The "v23.x" vs "v22.x" wording discrepancy between the two published copies of the 22.12.0 note (nodejs.org blog vs GitHub release tag) is unresolved from these sources alone; it does not affect the flags, the error code, or the feature check, which are identical in both copies.

Based on the source code of Prometheus's federation handler in `web/federate.go`, here is the breakdown of how native histograms and formats are handled:

---

### 1. Validity of the Claim
**The claim is not supported (it is false).** 

Not every selected native histogram can be emitted in every negotiated exposition format. Standard exponential native histograms cannot be emitted when a non-protobuf format (such as plain text `expfmt.TypeTextPlain`) is negotiated; in those cases, they are explicitly dropped/skipped from the response payload.

---

### 2. The Decisive Closed Skip Branch
The decisive skip logic occurs inside the sample serialization loop in `web/federate.go`, lines **190–203**:

```go
for _, s := range vec {
    isHistogram := s.H != nil
    formatType := format.FormatType()
    if isHistogram &&
        !s.H.UsesCustomBuckets() &&
        formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoDelim &&
        formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoText &&
        formatType != expfmt.TypeProtoCompact {
        // Can't serve a native histogram with a non-protobuf format.
        // (We can serve an NHCB, though, as it is converted to a
        // classic histogram for federation.)
        // TODO(codesome): Serve them when other protocols get the native histogram support.
        continue
    }
```

When this branch evaluates to true, the serializer executes `continue` (line 202), silently skipping the histogram sample without writing it to the output encoder.

---

### 3. Permitted Format Categories for Histograms Without Custom Buckets
For native histograms without custom buckets (`!s.H.UsesCustomBuckets()`), the guard condition permits emission **only** if the negotiated format is one of three Protobuf-based format categories (checked at `web/federate.go:195–197` against the formats negotiated in `web/federate.go:75` via `expfmt.NegotiateAccept`):

1. **Delimited Protocol Buffer:** `expfmt.TypeProtoDelim` (`application/vnd.google.protobuf; proto=io.prometheus.client.MetricFamily; encoding=delimited`)
2. **Protobuf Text Format:** `expfmt.TypeProtoText` (`application/vnd.google.protobuf; proto=io.prometheus.client.MetricFamily; encoding=text`)
3. **Compact Protobuf Text Format:** `expfmt.TypeProtoCompact` (`application/vnd.google.protobuf; proto=io.prometheus.client.MetricFamily; encoding=compact-text`)

If the negotiated format is the text format (`expfmt.TypeTextPlain`), the condition succeeds and the sample is bypassed.

---

### 4. Contrast with Custom-Bucket Histograms
Native histograms with custom buckets (NHCB, schema -53) are handled differently:
- **Skip Branch Bypassed:** For NHCBs, `s.H.UsesCustomBuckets()` evaluates to `true`, causing `!s.H.UsesCustomBuckets()` (line 194) to evaluate to `false`. As a result, the skip condition does not trigger, and NHCBs are **not** skipped even under non-protobuf formats like `expfmt.TypeTextPlain`.
- **Conversion to Classic Histogram:** Rather than encoding schema buckets as native histogram spans via `makeNativeHistogram` (`web/federate.go:300, 315–346`), NHCB samples branch at line 297–298 to call `makeClassicHistogram(s.H)` (`web/federate.go:350–378`). This translates the custom buckets into standard cumulative classic histogram buckets (`[]*dto.Bucket`). Because classic histograms are supported by the plain-text exposition format (which calculates and appends the `+Inf` bucket during text formatting; see lines 373–376), custom-bucket histograms can be federated across all negotiated formats.

---

### 5. Application to Ordinary Float Samples
**This restriction does not apply to ordinary float samples.**
- At `web/federate.go:191`, `isHistogram := s.H != nil`.
- For ordinary float samples, `s.H` is `nil`, meaning `isHistogram` is `false`.
- Because `isHistogram` is the first operand in the conjunction `if isHistogram && ...` (`web/federate.go:193`), the entire condition short-circuits to `false`.
- Float samples proceed through the loop and are encoded as `dto.Untyped` metrics (`web/federate.go:290–294`), which are fully supported across all negotiated exposition formats, including plain text.

---

### Unresolved Limitations
- While `expfmt.NegotiateAccept` in `web/federate.go:75` configures acceptance for `TypeProtoDelim`, `TypeProtoText`, `TypeProtoCompact`, and `TypeTextPlain`, the behavior if an unexpected custom format MIME type were somehow injected depends on underlying `expfmt` defaults.
- The comment at `web/federate.go:201` (`// TODO(codesome): Serve them when other protocols get the native histogram support`) notes future exposition protocols (e.g., OpenMetrics or newer Prometheus text formats supporting native histograms) may alter these restrictions in subsequent releases.

## Launch-time behavior (Node.js 22.0.0, April 2024)

The launch announcement says the release "adds `require()` support for synchronous ESM graphs under the flag **`--experimental-require-module`**" (contributed by Joyee Cheung, PR #51977). When that flag is enabled and the module being loaded by `require()` is explicitly marked as an ES module (a `"type": "module"` field in the closest `package.json` or a `.mjs` extension) and is fully synchronous (contains no top-level await), `require()` loads it as an ES Module and returns the module namespace object — similar to dynamic `import()` but run synchronously. The announcement explicitly says: "We intend to eventually enable `require(esm)` by default in the future, without the flag" — so at launch it was **not** on by default.

## What changed in exactly 22.12.0

The 22.12.0 release notes ("require(esm) is now enabled by default", commit `58d6871c45`, "module: unflag --experimental-require-module", PR #55085) reconcile with that promise:

- **Enabled by default in 22.12.0?** Yes. "Support for loading native ES modules using require() had been available on v20.x and v22.x under the command line flag `--experimental-require-module`... In this release, it is now no longer behind a flag on v22.x."
- **Does that make it stable?** No. The notes state: "This feature is still experimental, and we are looking for user feedback to make more final tweaks before fully stabilizing it." Being unflagged in 22.12.0 only removed the flag requirement; it did not change the stability status. (On v23.x an experimental warning is emitted unless `require()` comes from a `node_modules` path; the notes also note `--experimental-require-module` is checked separately from syntax detection.)

## Error for top-level await

With the feature enabled, Node.js no longer throws `ERR_REQUIRE_ESM` when `require()` loads an ES module. However, it "can, however, throw **`ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE`** if the ES module being loaded or its dependencies contain top-level `await`." This matches the launch announcement's requirement that the module graph be "fully synchronous (contains no top-level await)."

## Disabling flag and runtime feature check (documented for 22.12.0)

- **Disabling flag:** `--no-experimental-require-module` ("this feature can also be disabled using `--no-experimental-require-module` as a workaround" if regressions occur).
- **Runtime feature check:** `process.features.require_module` — "Users can check `process.features.require_module` to see whether `require(esm)` is enabled in the current Node.js instance." Additionally, for packages, the `"module-sync"` exports condition can be used to detect `require(esm)` support so both `require()` and `import` can load the same native ES module.

When `require()` of an ES module succeeds, the returned object is either an ES module namespace object (similar to `import()`) or whatever is exported as `"module.exports"` in the ES module (the `module.exports` interop export was added in 22.12.0, commit `545c069eb5`).

**Sources:**
- Node.js 22 launch announcement: https://nodejs.org/en/blog/announcements/v22-release-announce
- Node.js 22.12.0 (LTS) release notes: https://nodejs.org/en/blog/release/v22.12.0

**Limitation:** The 22.12.0 release-notes page was truncated in the commit listing (evidence budget), but all relevant "Notable Changes" text on require(esm) was captured in full; no behavior from any Node release later than 22.12.0 was used.

# Trace: `z.string().transform(fn)` in the assigned v4 classic API

Dispatch/evidence budget was exhausted before I could read the parse-entry bodies, so I cite only what I retrieved. Limitations are listed at the end.

## 1. Public builder → representation

`z.string()` calls `core._string(ZodString, params)` (`packages/zod/src/v4/classic/schemas.ts:617-621`), and `ZodString` initializes through `core.$ZodString.init` (`classic/schemas.ts:529-533`); the core string constructor installs the string parser and pattern (`packages/zod/src/v4/core/schemas.ts:399-420`).

`.transform(fn)` is declared on `ZodType` as returning `ZodPipe<this, ZodTransform<Awaited<NewOut>, core.output<this>>>` (`classic/schemas.ts:131-133`). Its implementation is:

```ts
transform(tx) { return pipe(this, transform(tx)); }   // classic/schemas.ts:245-247
```

`transform(fn)` builds `new ZodTransform({ type: "transform", transform: fn })` (`classic/schemas.ts:2291-2298`), and `pipe(in_, out)` builds `new ZodPipe({ type: "pipe", in: in_, out: out })` (`classic/schemas.ts:2555-2566`). The `ZodPipe` constructor calls `core.$ZodPipe.init` and `ZodType.init`, then stores `inst.in = def.in; inst.out = def.out` (`classic/schemas.ts:2546-2553`). `ZodTransform` calls `core.$ZodTransform.init` and `ZodType.init`, then overrides `inst._zod.parse` (`classic/schemas.ts:2249-2257`).

So the transformation is represented as two core defs: a `$ZodTransformDef` with `type: "transform"` and the callback `transform: (input, payload) => util.MaybeAsync<unknown>` (`core/schemas.ts:3824-3827`), and a `$ZodPipeDef` with `type: "pipe"`, `in`, `out`, whose optional `transform`/`reverseTransform` fields are documented as only defined inside `$ZodCodec` (`core/schemas.ts:4401-4409`). The string schema is the pipe's `in`; the transform is the pipe's `out`.

## 2. Order: input parse, then transform

In the forward direction, `$ZodPipe.parse` runs `const left = def.in._zod.run(payload, ctx)` and only then `handlePipeResult(left, def.out, ctx)` (`core/schemas.ts:4432-4446`). Inside `$ZodType`'s run wrapper, the base `inst._zod.parse` executes first and checks/refinements run after it (`core/schemas.ts:315-321`). For a string, `$ZodString.parse` coerces if `def.coerce`, accepts `typeof payload.value === "string"`, otherwise pushes `{ expected: "string", code: "invalid_type", input: payload.value, inst }` (`core/schemas.ts:403-418`). Thus the input is parsed (and checked) before the transform node is run.

`handlePipeResult` (`core/schemas.ts:4449-4457`) is the gate:

```ts
if (left.issues.some((iss) => iss.code !== "unrecognized_keys")) {
  left.aborted = true;
  return left;
}
return next._zod.run({ value: left.value, issues: left.issues }, ctx);
```

## 3. Which issues stop the pipe / code exception

The comment states it directly: "Any issue stops the pipe, so a failing refinement never feeds its transform. An unrecognized key is the exception…" (`core/schemas.ts:4450-4451`). Concretely, any issue whose `code` is not `"unrecognized_keys"` aborts: `left.aborted = true` and the left payload is returned, so the transform (`out`) is never invoked (`core/schemas.ts:4451-4455`). The single issue-code exception is `unrecognized_keys`, which is allowed through because it describes the input's extra properties rather than the piped value (`core/schemas.ts:4450`, `4451`).

## 4. Transform execution and carriage of the result

Because `ZodTransform` overwrites `_zod.parse`, the classic override executes (`classic/schemas.ts:2257-2287`). It throws `core.$ZodEncodeError(inst.constructor.name)` when `_ctx.direction === "backward"` (`2258-2260`), installs `payload.addIssue` (`2262-2276`), then calls `const output = def.transform(payload.value, payload)` (`2278`). For a Promise it returns `output.then((output) => { payload.value = output; return payload; })` (`2279-2284`); for a sync value it does `payload.value = output; return payload;` (`2285-2286`).

The core `$ZodTransform.parse` is equivalent but additionally handles `ctx.async` and throws `core.$ZodAsyncError()` if a Promise arrives when not async (`core/schemas.ts:3844-3864`; sync assignment at `3862-3863`). The result is carried onward by mutation of the shared payload: the transform writes the transformed value into `payload.value`, and `handlePipeResult` had already passed `{ value: left.value, issues: left.issues }` into `next._zod.run`, so the same payload object flows out (`core/schemas.ts:4456`). The core sync entry sets `{ async: false }` (`core/parse.ts:22-24`), with `parse = _parse(errors.$ZodRealError)` exported at `core/parse.ts:39`.

## Unresolved limitations

- Budget expired before reading `core/parse.ts` past line 24 or `classic/parse.ts` at all; therefore the top-level unwrapping of `payload.value` into the final parse/safeParse result and error construction are not source-cited.
- The timing of the deferred `inst._zod.run = inst._zod.parse` assignment for no-check schemas (`core/schemas.ts:226-231`) was not verified against the code that drains `_zod.deferred`; I can only cite that the deferred callback is registered.
- The exact installed snapshot version was not read from `package.json`.
